title: Argireline and Matrixyl 3000 together: what the trials show
seo_title: Matrixyl and Argireline: What the Trials Show
seo_description: Matrixyl and Argireline together: no trial has tested the pair. See what each one's own studies show and how to layer them with care.
summary: No study has tested Argireline and Matrixyl 3000 together, so this article sets out what each peptide's own trials show, how to layer the two, and who should be careful.
body_html:
The short answers on Matrixyl and Argireline:

  • Do they work together? Nobody knows. No study has tested Argireline and Matrixyl 3000 as a pair, so we cannot say they add up to more than either alone. They do different jobs, and each has its own trials.
  • Which goes first? No trial has tested the order either. The practical rule is the thinnest product first, then the richer one, and one new product at a time.
  • Who should skip? Anyone who is pregnant or breastfeeding should ask a doctor or pharmacist first, because neither peptide has been tested in those groups. Patch-test before using either.

This article draws on the trials we appraise on our two research pages: Acetyl Hexapeptide-8 (Argireline) research and Matrixyl 3000 research. Everything below is checked against those sources.

Do Argireline and Matrixyl 3000 work together?

There is no published study of Matrixyl and Argireline used together. We looked, and we would rather say so plainly than imply otherwise. Any claim that the two multiply each other’s effect would have nothing behind it.

What exists is separate evidence for each peptide. It is worth knowing what each one was actually tested on.

Argireline® (acetyl hexapeptide-8) is a peptide designed to soften the look of expression lines, such as crow’s feet and forehead lines. Two trials used 10% Argireline, the same level as in our serum:

  • In a double-blind trial of 60 adults (Wang 2013), clinicians graded the crow’s feet of 22 of the 45 people using Argireline as clearly smoother after 4 weeks. None of the 15 people on placebo were graded that way. Note that 22 of 45 counts people, not a percentage of wrinkle removed.
  • In a small trial of 24 women (Raikou 2017), forehead roughness measured by instrument fell 7.4% after 20 days on Argireline, while it rose 4.3% on placebo.

Matrixyl® 3000 is a pair of peptides, palmitoyl tripeptide-1 and palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7, made by the company Sederma. Its human data comes from the manufacturer, not from independent researchers:

  • In the manufacturer’s 2-month half-face study of 23 women aged 42 to 67, the area taken up by deep wrinkles fell 39.4% on the treated side. The placebo side showed no significant change.
  • In lab tests on skin cells, the two peptides together raised collagen I by 256% at the highest dose tested, against cells given only the solvent. That is a cell result, not a measurement in skin.

Why are they different jobs?

Argireline’s trials looked at expression lines, the creases that form around the eyes and forehead as you move your face. Matrixyl 3000’s trials looked at deep wrinkles and the look of firmness.

That is the reason people consider using both. It is a sensible idea, but it is an idea, not a result. “Together” can mean two things here. It can mean two products that each do their own job, which is what the evidence supports. It cannot yet mean a proven combined effect. Neither trial tested what happens when the other peptide is on the skin too.

Which goes first, and how do you layer them?

Neither peptide is an acid or a retinoid, so they do not need to be kept apart the way strong exfoliating acids do. Our Matrixyl 3000 hub makes the same point: they can be layered, one new product at a time. A sensible routine looks like this:

  • Thinnest first. Apply the lighter, more watery product to clean skin, then the richer one over it. Serum goes before cream.
  • Morning and evening. Both were used twice a day in the trials above.
  • SPF every morning. Sunscreen goes on last. Peptides do not replace it.
  • Introduce one product at a time. Start one, wait a week or two, then add the other. If your skin reacts, you will know which one caused it.
  • Patch-test first. Put a small amount on the inner forearm or behind the ear for a day or two before using it on your face.
  • Give it time. The trials ran from 20 days to 2 months. Judge the result after weeks, not days.

No trial has compared one order against the other, so we do not claim that order changes the result. It is about comfort and keeping your routine simple.

Who should skip or be careful?

Neither of our products has been through its own tolerance test, so we do not describe them as suitable for sensitive skin. What we can report is ingredient-level:

  • Argireline caused no adverse effects in the two controlled trials above (Wang 2013 and Raikou 2017).
  • An independent expert panel, the Cosmetic Ingredient Review, assessed both Matrixyl 3000 peptides as safe in cosmetics at current use levels. That is a finding about the ingredients, not about any one finished product.

Be careful, or ask first, if any of these apply:

  • Pregnant or breastfeeding. Neither peptide has been tested in these groups. Ask a doctor or pharmacist before use.
  • Broken, sunburnt or inflamed skin. Wait until it has settled.
  • Stinging or redness that does not fade. Stop using the product.
  • Needles of any kind. These serums are for the skin’s surface only. Never inject Argireline, and never use it with DIY microneedling. An infection has been reported after Argireline was injected.

What do our products contain?

  • Acetyl Hexapeptide-8 Anti-Wrinkle Serum contains 10% Argireline®. That is 10% of the Argireline peptide solution, not 10% pure peptide, and it is the level used in the trials above.
  • Matrixyl 3000 Firming Serum contains Matrixyl 3000 and also palmitoyl pentapeptide-4, a related peptide.
  • Matrixyl 3000 Pro-Collagen Firming Cream contains Matrixyl 3000. It does not contain palmitoyl pentapeptide-4.
  • The Fine Lines & Wrinkles Peptide Duo Set pairs the Matrixyl 3000 and Acetyl Hexapeptide-8 serums for people who want to try both.

The trials in this article tested the ingredients, not our finished products. We have not tested our serums ourselves, so we cannot say our products will give the same results.
